source.title: Unify Variables in Neural Scaling Laws for General Audio Representations via Embedding Effective Rank
source.authors: Xu-Yao Deng; Yan-Jie Sun; Yong Dou; Ke-Le Xu

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Figure contents are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to general audio representation learning, using RankMe and HEAR performance rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study measures audio representation quality and reports scaling trends for RankMe and HEAR scores. It does not measure held-out language-model loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The reported fitting parameters are not numerically given in the text; several plotted values are figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study fits power-law-plus-constant laws of downstream audio quality (HEAR) against parameters, data hours and compute for masked-autoencoder audio models. That bears on V5 (other modalities) and, for audio, on V6. It never measures language-model pretraining loss, so V1–V4 and V7 are not tested as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' central claim is that embedding effective rank (RankMe) unifies diverse variables into one power law with HEAR quality. They say this validates classical scaling principles in audio, and they report conventional N, D and C power-law-plus-constant laws with saturation ceilings below 1.
record.recipe_differences: Uses RankMe and HEAR downstream scores for self-supervised audio representations rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy and language-model compute-optimal fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted RankMe-to-HEAR parameters differ between converged and compute-constrained checkpoint sets; architecture settings and data volume also change reported outcomes. The authors attribute fit differences to the number and quality of data points.

fits_no_version.finding: Early RankMe correlates with HEAR at 700k steps across 45 models (PCC 0.636 at 50k rising to 0.862 at 300k).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early audio-embedding effective rank predicts later downstream audio representation performance.

fits_no_version.finding: HEAR follows a power law in RankMe across many checkpoints, masking rates and architectures. The fitted parameters differ between converged and compute-constrained checkpoint sets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding effective rank is a unified power-law predictor of audio representation quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Audio models with similar parameter counts but different width and depth can differ markedly in HEAR (figure-only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For audio MAE encoders, architecture shape at fixed parameters matters for downstream quality.

record.problems: The study concerns audio representation learning, not language-model held-out loss. Several scaling curves and their values are available only in figures, and fitted coefficients and their uncertainty are not reported in the text. The study does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its architecture comparisons involve differences in pretraining methods and datasets as well as model size.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 8 presents separate task-level RankMe scaling curves for 16 HEAR tasks, but the supplied text does not expose task-specific values or a reliable task-to-curve assignment; the paper's aggregate textual statement about these tasks is covered in R1. Other figure-only details not bearing on the tested versions were not extracted.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss is measured. The validation MSE is monitored but not analysed.
No fits on small runs are used to predict much larger runs. The early-RankMe correlation is a different predictor and target.
No loss-minimising parameter/token split at fixed compute is reported. There is only a qualitative remark that larger models trained for fewer steps are more efficient, made for audio.
No language-model loss is compared across shapes at fixed parameter count.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes are untested. Audio pretraining loss itself is not fitted; only downstream HEAR is.
Language-model downstream tasks are untested, as is prediction from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or of disagreement between published laws for N/D/C laws.

missing.what: Masking rate effect on HEAR is non-monotonic for en768-12 on 5,333 h. This bears on RankMe only, not on V-scaling.
Per-task Q∞, RC and αR differences across the 16 HEAR tasks; some tasks plateau early.

record.verdict_notes: All N/D/C scaling results are figure-only, and fitted coefficients are not given. The architecture comparison (Table V) confounds size with pretraining data and method. The audio results bear on V5 and V6 via downstream HEAR, not pretraining loss.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss of language models, or its power-law scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit power laws to small runs and test predictions of much larger runs. Its early-RankMe prediction experiments use a different predictor and target.
No fixed-compute loss-minimising allocation between parameter count and training tokens is measured.
Architecture configurations are varied, but the study does not test whether architecture details change language-model loss only slightly at fixed parameter count.
Tests general audio representation learning, not image/video models, language-model loss, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer training regimes.
Tests downstream HEAR performance for audio models, not language-model downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.

Reports setup-dependent fits and audio-model performance differences, but does not test LLM parameter-counting choices, LLM training schedules or data, or whether compute-optimal allocations vary with fitting choices.
